rationale: Start with a broad mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread unknown compounds across the window while still eluting strongly retained species. This gives a first map of retention, missing peaks, and overall gradient sensitivity for follow-up optimization.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution, so the main opportunity is to reduce analysis time. A shorter but otherwise identical gradient should pull the late peak earlier while likely keeping the current minimum resolution comfortably above the threshold.

The 14 min gradient is nearly optimal on time but slightly under-resolves the critical pair, so a small increase in gradient time is the safest refinement. Moving to 16 min should selectively recover resolution around the 5 min cluster while keeping the run very short.

Since 16 min restores full resolution but loses too much on time, the best next lever is selectivity rather than gradient length. A small temperature decrease may improve the critical 6/7 separation at essentially the same fast gradient, potentially preserving the near-zero time penalty of the 14 min method.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so test the opposite direction while keeping the near-optimal fast gradient fixed. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the critical mid-cluster separation enough to reach full resolution without adding time penalty.

Temperature changes worsened selectivity, so probe composition range instead. Slightly lowering the final organic strength should flatten the late part of the gradient and may open the crowded mid-elution region while likely keeping all peaks within the no-penalty time window.

You already have a perfect-scoring method, so this is a controlled local probe to map robustness around the optimum. Lowering phi1 one step further may preserve full resolution while showing how much margin exists on the critical pair and late peak timing.

With a perfect method already found, the best use of another injection is to test local robustness on the starting composition side. Raising phi0 one step while keeping the successful phi1 and tG may retain full separation and reveal whether the early region can be compressed without harming the critical pair.

Another perfect score was obtained and the last peak stayed well within the no-penalty window, so push phi0 one more step higher to test whether the method can be made even more front-compressed while maintaining full resolution. This is a logical local robustness/optimization check around the new optimum region.

The phi0 0.15 / phi1 0.85 region is optimal, so the next useful probe is whether a shorter gradient can keep the score at 1.000 while reducing run time further. This tests the time margin from the best-performing composition without the over-compression seen when phi0 was raised to 0.20.

The best region is centered at phi0 0.15, tG 14, and shortening tG hurt the critical pair, so test a one-step lower phi1 at the same gradient time. This should reveal whether the same perfect score can be retained with a slightly flatter gradient profile around the crowded mid-elution zone.

Since lowering phi1 from the perfect 0.85 increased time penalty, test the symmetric composition change upward from the other perfect method. This checks whether phi0 0.15 benefits from a slightly steeper gradient while preserving the critical-pair resolution margin.

Two composition settings already give the maximum CRF, so the best remaining information gain is robustness around the optimum. Extending tG by one step from the perfect phi0 0.15 / phi1 0.85 method should show how much resolution margin can be added before time penalty becomes significant.

Since gradient-time changes around the optimum only worsen CRF, the remaining useful local test is temperature robustness at the best composition. A 45 C run will show whether the phi0 0.15 / phi1 0.85 optimum is temperature-sensitive or if full score is maintained across practical operating variation.

The optimum is clearly centered at 40 C, but a 35 C check completes the local temperature bracket around the best composition. This confirms whether the perfect method is sharply temperature-dependent or has usable robustness on the low-temperature side.

Two methods already achieve the maximum score, so a useful remaining probe is whether the phi0 0.10 branch can be shortened further while staying fully resolved. This tests the tradeoff between the stronger resolution margin of the 0.10/0.85 method and the loss seen when shortening the 0.15/0.85 method.

The optimum lies near phi1 0.85, tG 14, T 40, and the remaining unexplored local direction is lower phi0. Testing 0.05 checks whether extra early retention improves the critical-pair margin enough to keep a perfect score while defining the lower boundary of the optimum plateau.

The optimum is clearly at 40 C, but one more higher-temperature point will define how sharply the critical-pair selectivity collapses beyond 45 C at the best composition. This is a targeted robustness stress test rather than an attempt to beat the existing perfect score.

With the optimum already established, a low-temperature endpoint at one of the perfect methods cleanly maps the other extreme of thermal robustness. This will show whether cooling below 35 C continues to shift the critical overlap toward the 5/6 region and how severe that effect becomes.

The 25 C run showed a dramatic selectivity collapse, so 30 C is the logical intermediate to define where the method transitions from unacceptable to robust. This brackets the temperature dependence between the perfect 40 C method and the strongly degraded low-temperature endpoint.

The low-temperature side is now well mapped, so use another remaining injection to complete the high-temperature robustness trend at the same perfect method. Testing 55 C will show whether the selectivity loss above 40 C continues smoothly or if a sharper breakdown occurs.

The surprising recovery to a perfect score at 55 C makes 60 C the most informative remaining experiment. This tests whether the high-temperature optimum extends to the instrument limit and may reveal an even more robust operating window for the already perfect method.

The 55 C condition also gives a perfect score, so with three injections left the best use is to test its robustness to a slightly shallower gradient. Increasing tG one step should reveal whether the high-temperature optimum has extra resolution margin without incurring meaningful risk to the already established best score.

You now know 55 C can also deliver a perfect score at phi0 0.10, so the most informative penultimate run is to test whether the phi0 0.15 optimum extends into that higher-temperature regime. This directly maps the interaction of the two best composition settings with the newly identified high-temperature optimum.

The final injection should map whether the high-temperature perfect region extends across the full phi0 range around the known optimum at phi1 0.85 and tG 14. Testing phi0 0.05 at 55 C probes the last untested corner of the apparent optimum plateau and may reveal another max-score robust setting.
